questions.q: Which algorithm allows short bursts of traffic while still enforcing a long-term average request rate?
options: Fixed window counter
Sliding window log
Token bucket
Leaky bucket with a constant drain rate

questions.q: What is the main weakness of the fixed window counter algorithm?
options: Bursts straddling a window boundary can pass nearly double the limit
It requires storing a separate timestamp for every single request in the window
It cannot be implemented with simple key expiry in Redis
It drains requests at a constant rate regardless of load

questions.q: What is the defining behavior of the leaky bucket algorithm?
options: It refills credits at a fixed rate and lets accumulated bursts pass through
It emits requests at a constant rate, smoothing bursts through a queue
It counts requests in discrete non-overlapping time intervals
It stores one timestamp per request for exact rolling accounting

questions.q: Which HTTP status code should a rate limiter return when a client exceeds its quota?
options: 403 Forbidden
503 Service Unavailable
401 Unauthorized
429 Too Many Requests

questions.q: What does the Retry-After response header communicate to a throttled client?
options: How many requests remain available in the current window
How long the client should wait before sending its next request
Which rate limit tier applies to the client's API key
The timestamp when the server last reset all of its rate-limit counters globally

questions.q: Where is a rate limiter typically placed in a service architecture?
options: In an API gateway or middleware before requests reach application logic
Inside each database shard, throttling queries after business logic runs
Only in client SDKs, trusting each caller to self-throttle honestly
In the TLS termination handshake before any HTTP parsing occurs

questions.q: What does the sliding window log algorithm store for each client?
options: A single counter that resets at fixed intervals
A token count plus the time of the last refill
A timestamp for every request inside the current window
A weighted average of the request counts from the previous two windows

questions.q: How does the sliding window counter algorithm approximate a rolling limit cheaply?
options: It keeps per-request timestamps but compresses them into buckets
It slowly drains a queue of pending requests at a constant rate configured per client key
It resets its counter early whenever traffic briefly drops to zero
It blends the previous window's count, weighted by overlap, with the current count

questions.q: Each API node keeps rate-limit counters in local memory behind a round-robin load balancer. What is the consequence?
options: The effective global limit becomes roughly N times the intended limit across N nodes
Requests get rejected roughly N times more often than the configured rate-limit policy intends
Counting stays accurate because round-robin spreads each client's load evenly
Latency rises sharply because nodes must synchronize on every request

questions.q: Why implement check-and-increment as a Lua script in Redis rather than separate commands?
options: Lua bytecode executes measurably faster than native Redis commands
The script runs atomically, preventing races between concurrent check-and-increment operations
Lua lets counters shard themselves across cluster slots automatically
Redis persists Lua results to disk so counters survive restarts

questions.q: A team implements the limit check as a GET followed by a separate INCR call. Under high concurrency, what happens?
options: Redis pipelines the two calls together so no race can occur
The second call fails because Redis locks the key after a read
Requests serialize on the key, doubling latency but keeping the count strictly correct
Concurrent clients can both read a stale count and slip past the limit

questions.q: A rate limiter's Redis backend goes down and the limiter is configured to fail open. What results?
options: All requests are rejected until the Redis backend fully recovers
Requests queue inside the limiter until counters become reachable again
All traffic passes unthrottled, preserving availability but losing overload protection
The limiter falls back to exact sliding-window logs kept locally

questions.q: For a login endpoint, should the rate limiter fail open or fail closed when its backing store is unreachable?
options: Fail closed, since unlimited attempts would enable credential-stuffing attacks
Fail open, since login availability always outweighs any abuse risk
Fail open, because authentication servers already throttle failed attempts themselves downstream
Neither one; disable login rate limits and rely entirely on CAPTCHAs

questions.q: An API sees abuse from many accounts behind one corporate NAT. What would limiting by IP address alone do?
options: Have no effect, because NAT rewrites source ports rather than addresses
Stop the abusive accounts precisely with no collateral impact on anyone
Only work if the limiter is deployed at the CDN edge locations
Punish legitimate users who share that IP along with the abusers

questions.q: A token bucket has capacity 100 and refills at 10 tokens per second. What traffic does it permit?
options: Bursts of at most 10 requests at a time, with a sustained rate of 100 per second
Bursts up to 100 requests at once, with a sustained rate of 10 per second
Exactly 100 requests per second at all times regardless of history
Up to 110 requests every second until the bucket fully empties

questions.q: A service wants approximately global rate limiting while adding minimal latency to each request. What is the best approach?
options: Run synchronous consensus through a Raft quorum on every request
Guard a single SQL counter row with SELECT FOR UPDATE per request
Keep local counters and sync deltas to a shared store periodically, accepting small overshoot
Fan out each request to every peer node and wait for agreement

questions.q: When does the sliding window counter's weighted estimate misjudge traffic the most?
options: When traffic is perfectly uniform across both measured windows
When the window length is configured much larger than one second
When the counters live in Redis rather than in local node memory
When previous-window requests clustered near one edge, breaking the uniformity assumption

questions.q: Why can a multi-key rate-limiting Lua script fail when moved from a single Redis node to Redis Cluster?
options: Its keys can hash to different slots, and scripts require all keys in one slot
Cluster mode disables Lua scripting entirely for consistency reasons
Scripts cannot run on replicas, and cluster mode always routes reads to replicas
EVAL loses its atomicity guarantee in cluster mode, reintroducing races

questions.q: Why is a sliding window log prohibitively expensive at 10 million clients sending 100 requests per minute each?
options: Each lookup costs O(n log n) time, saturating CPU long before memory matters
It keeps around a billion timestamps in memory, versus one or two counters per client
Redis caps sorted sets at one million entries per key, forcing key splitting
The timestamps must be replicated synchronously to every node in the cluster

questions.q: Thousands of throttled clients receive 429 responses carrying identical Retry-After values. What failure follows, and what is the standard fix?
options: Retries interleave naturally over time, so no fix is actually needed
Connections stay pinned open awaiting retry, which is fixed by shortening keep-alive timeouts
A synchronized retry spike arrives all at once; adding jitter to retry delays spreads it
DNS caches expire simultaneously across clients, fixed by lengthening record TTLs
